worksheet.title: The Mismatched Message
worksheet.subtitle: The messages don't match — fix the link
worksheet.learning_goal: I can find why a message does not start a script and fix the words so they match.

parts.title: Pixel never hears it
parts.text: Bit (green) starts on the green flag and sends a message. Pixel (purple) waits for a message. Pixel is supposed to reach 3 — but it never moves! Look closely: the word Bit SENDS and the word Pixel WAITS FOR are not the same. Find the mismatched message and fix it.

parts.title: Run it — what goes wrong?
parts.prompt: Click the flag. Where does Bit land? Does Pixel move at all? Circle YES or NO. What number is Pixel on?

parts.title: Find the mismatch
parts.prompt: Write the two messages. Bit broadcasts '____'. Pixel waits for '____'. Are they the same word? Why doesn't Pixel start?

parts.title: Fix it
parts.prompt: Change ONE message so they match. Write Pixel's fixed hat (or Bit's fixed broadcast). After the fix, where does Pixel land?

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: A 'when I receive' script only starts if the broadcast message is EXACTLY the word it waits for. Here Bit sent 'go' but Pixel waited for 'stop', so Pixel never started. Make the two messages the same word and Pixel runs to its goal.

teacher_guide.eyebrow: Teacher Guide · Grade 2 · Debugging & Reading Code
teacher_guide.title: The Mismatched Message
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key

parts.title: Goal
parts.text: Students debug a broken EVENT link in concurrent code (C3.2 read/alter + C3.1 write). Pixel never starts because its receive hat ('when I receive stop') does not match Bit's broadcast ('go'). Students compare the two message words, see they differ, and fix one so they match. Debugging message mismatches is a key reading skill for event-driven concurrent code.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum (Grade 2 — C3 Coding)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.

parts.title: Materials
parts.text: The printed worksheet and a pencil. Optional: two message cards reading 'go' and 'stop'; hold them side by side to show they do not match, then change one.

parts.title: Run it (about 20 min)
text: 1. I DO: run it — 'Bit goes 0 forward 1 → 1 and broadcasts go. But Pixel is waiting for stop, so it never hears its message.'
2. WE DO: compare the words — 'go' vs 'stop'. Different, so Pixel's hat never fires; it stays at 5.
3. YOU DO: students fix one message so both say the same word, then run Pixel: 5 back 2 → 3.
4. Connect: 'A receive hat needs the EXACT message it waits for — check the words match.'

parts.title: Answer key (modelled by the run-gate)
text: Ex 1 — Bit: 0 → forward 1 → 1. Pixel does NOT move (circle NO); it stays on its home number 5.
Ex 2 — Bit broadcasts 'go'; Pixel waits for 'stop'. They are NOT the same word, so Pixel's receive event never fires.
Ex 3 — fix: change Pixel's hat to 'when I receive go' (or Bit's broadcast to 'stop'). With matching messages, Pixel runs: 5 → back 2 → 3.
Fix note: either edit works as long as BOTH messages end up the same word; then Pixel reaches its goal 3.

parts.title: Watch for & differentiate
text: Common error: changing a move block — the bug is the EVENT message, not Pixel's motion.
Simplify: have students circle the two message words and check letter by letter if they match.
Extend: ask what happens if Bit's 'broadcast go' block is deleted (Pixel never starts no matter what its hat says).
Success indicator: the child reports Pixel stuck at 5, names the message mismatch, and fixes a message so Pixel reaches 3.
